message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless the landlord gives a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you paid.
• Request a written receipt when you hand over keys. | | **Habitability** | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to keep premises safe, sanitary, and fit for habitation (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical).
• If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | • Document problems with photos and dates.
• Give the landlord written notice and a reasonable time to fix the issue. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease termination by landlord: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month tenants; 60‑day notice for longer leases.
• For lease termination by tenant: 30‑day notice (or as specified in the lease). | • Use certified mail or a reliable delivery service to prove notice was received. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must file a complaint in district court and serve you with a summons and complaint.
• You have 5 days to respond (file an answer).
• If you fail to respond, the court may issue a judgment for possession. | • Respond promptly; consider hiring an attorney or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but the increase must be in writing and given at least 30 days before it takes effect. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords must not interfere with your peaceful use of the property. | • If a landlord repeatedly enters without notice, you may sue for damages. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to fix, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the condition before and after repairs. | | **Lease Termination** | • You can terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability) and the breach is not cured after notice. | • Provide written notice of the breach and a reasonable cure period. | | **Tenant Insurance** | • While not required by law, it’s wise to carry renters insurance to protect personal belongings and liability. | • Shop around for policies that cover theft, fire, and accidental damage. | ### Quick Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes, consumer complaints, and legal forms. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance, mediation services, and educational workshops. | | **District Court Clerk’s Office** | Guidance on filing complaints, serving notices, and court procedures. | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely notice before eviction or rent increases, protection against discrimination, and the ability to withhold rent or repair and deduct if the landlord fails to meet obligations. Always keep written records, give proper notice, and seek professional help if you encounter serious disputes.
